paras.text: Appraisal and Suit Limits — Audio Lecture

Welcome to the appraisal and suit limits chapter. This is the part of Michigan insurance law that resolves fights over money: the machine that turns a disagreement into a number, and the clock that forces everybody to move. Two ideas run through all of it. First, appraisal decides how much is owed, never whether it is owed. Second, the one year suit clock is less scary than it sounds, because it stops running while the carrier is still working the claim.

Let's start with the statute. M C L five hundred point two eight three three, subsection one m, is the appraisal clause every Michigan fire insurance policy must contain. If the insured and insurer cannot agree on the actual cash value or the amount of the loss, either side can send a written demand that the amount be set by appraisal. Once that demand is received, each party has twenty days to pick a competent, independent appraiser and tell the other side who it is. The two appraisers then try to agree on a competent, impartial umpire. Notice those two different words. Party appraisers only have to be independent, meaning not controlled by the other side. The umpire has to be impartial, neutral to both. That distinction matters later, so hold onto it.

If the two appraisers cannot agree on an umpire within fifteen days, either side can ask a judge of the circuit court, in the county where the loss happened or where the property sits, to pick one. The appraisers then set the amount of the loss and the actual cash value item by item, not as one lump sum, which is exactly why a good line item estimate with photographs is the right document to bring into an appraisal. If they cannot agree within what the statute calls a reasonable time, and that phrase is never defined anywhere, no number of days, no case that sets one, they hand their differences to the umpire. Whatever any two of the three sign in writing is the binding amount of the loss. Each side pays for its own appraiser. The umpire's fee and other appraisal expenses split fifty fifty. There is no loser pays rule here.

Now the single most important idea in this chapter. Appraisal decides amount, never coverage. The leading case is Auto Owners Insurance Company versus Kwaiser, from nineteen ninety one, a published Court of Appeals opinion describing appraisal as a simple and inexpensive method for the prompt adjustment and settlement of claims, essentially a stand in for a lawsuit about dollar amounts. But Kwaiser also draws the line. If the parties cannot agree on coverage itself, a court decides that first, in a declaratory action, before any appraiser touches the file. The flip side, that once an insurer admits a loss is covered a court is statutorily required to send the parties into appraisal, is not actually a Kwaiser line. That sentence comes from a federal case called The D Boys, and the Michigan Court of Appeals adopted it word for word in the published Cantina opinion, which is what makes it binding here. The Michigan Supreme Court said the same thing in Dupree versus Auto Owners Insurance Company in twenty fourteen: while matters of coverage are generally determined by the courts, the method of determining the loss is reserved for the appraisers.
So how do you tell, in a real file, whether you are looking at a coverage fight or an amount of loss fight? Two recent cases answer that, and you need both, because the second narrows the first.

The first case is Cantina Enterprises Two Incorporated versus Property Owners Insurance Company, a published two thousand twenty four decision. A restaurant kitchen caught fire. The carrier never disputed that the fire was covered. It argued about whether certain items counted as the tenant's improvements and betterments and kept asking for more paperwork, but at the same time it started paying, including thirty thousand dollars toward the disputed category. The Court of Appeals sided with the insured. By paying on the claim and never formally denying liability, the carrier admitted the fire was covered, so the only question left, how much of the disputed betterments were owed, was an amount of loss question for the appraisers. Cantina has a second lesson too: the carrier waived the policy's sixty day proof of loss deadline by twice extending its own document requests and continuing to accept paperwork past that deadline.

For years, policyholder lawyers read Cantina broadly, as if any partial payment on any claim automatically opened the whole file to appraisal. Then, in February of twenty twenty six, the Court of Appeals published Maksym versus Auto Owners Insurance Company and drew the line much tighter. In Maksym, a pipe broke in a second floor bathroom and damaged the kitchen below. The carrier's first letter confirmed coverage for the water damage from the leaking pipe, but in the same letter expressly denied coverage for the plumbing repairs themselves and for additional living expenses. Over the following months the carrier paid about ten thousand dollars for the specific kitchen items it accepted, while repeatedly saying it was still denying the plumbing claims. The insureds demanded appraisal on their entire one hundred thirty five thousand dollar claim, arguing Cantina entitled them to it.

The Court of Appeals said no, and read Cantina's holding as far narrower than the insureds argued. The key difference: the carrier in Cantina never formally denied liability, it just wanted more proof. The carrier in Maksym paid for the specific items it determined were covered while expressly disputing liability for the others. That is not a partial payment on the disputed claims, that is payment on the accepted claims plus an actual denial on the rest. So there was no appraisal on the denied items, because whether they were covered at all remained disputed. The rule: paying the parts you agree on while expressly denying the rest is not an admission on the denied parts. Those need a coverage decision first, whether by negotiation, a carve out, or a lawsuit.

That raises the next question. How do you know, from reading a letter, whether something has actually been formally denied? This matters twice over, because a formal denial both takes an item out of appraisal and restarts the one year suit clock. The controlling language comes from Smitham versus State Farm Fire and Casualty Company, from two thousand twelve, quoted directly in Maksym: a formal denial must be explicit, and must unequivocally impress upon the insured the need to go to court. In Maksym, the carrier's first letter clearly denied the plumbing claim. But that same letter, on the second floor bathroom and other kitchen items, only asked for more documentation and warned coverage may be jeopardized. The Court of Appeals said that language was not explicit or unequivocal and sent the case back down, because a single letter can formally deny some items while leaving others open. Read every carrier letter line by line. Smitham adds the partial payment rule, worth remembering when you are chasing supplements: the insured's awareness of how much the carrier paid is not itself a formal denial. To restart the clock, the carrier has to say in no uncertain terms that it is denying all liability in excess of what it has already paid.

Now the suit clock itself. M C L five hundred point two eight three three, subsection one q, says an action under the policy must be commenced within one year after the loss, or within the time period specified in the policy, whichever is longer. So it is not always exactly a year, if the policy itself grants more time, the longer period wins. And here is the part that should make you breathe easier: the statute tolls, meaning it pauses, the running of that clock from the time the insured notifies the insurer of the loss until the insurer formally denies liability. This is not a brand new invention of the legislature. It goes back to a nineteen seventy six Michigan Supreme Court case, Tom Thomas Organization versus Reliance Insurance Company. A film and tape company lost property, the policy gave twelve months to sue, and the insurer argued the clock ran from the date of loss. The Supreme Court disagreed, holding that the appropriate resolution was to toll the running of the limitation from the time the insured gives notice until the insurer formally denies liability. Notice went out around January of nineteen seventy two, the insurer denied liability in June of that year, and because those five months did not count against the twelve month clock, the lawsuit filed the following March came in on time. The legislature did not write this section into the Insurance Code until nineteen ninety, fourteen years after Tom Thomas, so the courts had already built the tolling rule by hand before the legislature codified it. The rule is older than the statute that now contains it.

Two traps live inside Tom Thomas, and you need both. First, Tom Thomas did not hold that a one year deadline is unreasonable or unconscionable. The Court said in so many words that it was unnecessary to reach that argument, and rested its holding on tolling instead. If you ever see that sentence quoted without the word not, the source has inverted the holding. Second, Tom Thomas is partly overruled. In Rory versus Continental Insurance Company, a two thousand five Michigan Supreme Court case, the Court said that to the degree Tom Thomas and its progeny abrogate unambiguous contractual terms on the basis of reasonableness determinations, they are overruled. That reaches only the reasonableness talk. The tolling holding survives, and for fire policies it now lives in the statute anyway.

Rory itself is the case on how hard Michigan courts enforce a clear deadline. Two claimants sued their own auto insurer for uninsured motorist benefits about sixteen months after the accident, past a one year policy deadline, and the lower courts refused to enforce it as unreasonable. The Supreme Court reversed: a court must construe and apply unambiguous contract provisions as written, and a mere judicial assessment of reasonableness is an invalid basis to refuse to enforce a contract provision. Only a violation of law, or a traditional contract defense like fraud, duress, waiver, estoppel or unconscionability, can set a clear provision aside. But do not carry Rory too far into a fire claim. Rory was uninsured motorist coverage, so subsection one q was not in play. In a fire policy the statute sets a floor, and a second statute, M C L five hundred point two eight six zero, makes any fire policy provision contrary to that chapter absolutely void. Smitham used exactly that statute to strike a policy that tried to make tolling conditional on a formal denial.

Two more pieces round out this chapter. First, can a homeowner's own appraiser be paid a percentage of the recovery, the way a public adjuster often is? Yes. White versus State Farm Fire and Casualty Company, a published two thousand eleven case, held that a contingency fee does not disqualify a party appraiser from being independent, because independent is not the same standard as impartial, and a party appraiser is allowed to advocate for the side that picked them, much like an attorney. The one condition: the opposing party has to be told the contingency fee arrangement exists. Disclose it in the demand letter and you are fine.

Second, once an appraisal award is signed, how hard is it to undo? Very hard. Kwaiser set the standard and Dupree versus Auto Owners Insurance Company confirmed it: judicial review of an appraisal award is limited to bad faith, fraud, misconduct, or manifest mistake, the same narrow standard courts use for arbitration awards. Dupree teaches a second lesson on the same facts. An award stating an actual cash value figure does not by itself entitle the insured to the replacement cost holdback, the depreciation withheld until repairs are completed. That insured had an award of over a hundred twenty eight thousand dollars in actual cash value and nearly forty thousand in calculated depreciation, but because she never proved she replaced the property, the Supreme Court held she was not owed the depreciation on top of the ACV number.

Let's walk a restoration example. A hailstorm hits a Michigan roof. The contractor writes a full replacement estimate and the homeowner submits it with a signed proof of loss on day zero. By day thirty the carrier agrees the storm is covered but pays only for a small patch on one slope, saying the rest of the roof needs more documentation. That letter is not a formal denial under Smitham, so under Cantina this file sits on the appraisal track: coverage admitted, only scope in dispute. On day forty five the homeowner sends a written appraisal demand, names a competent, independent appraiser, and discloses any contingency fee right in the letter, following White. Day sixty five, twenty days later, is the carrier's deadline to name its own appraiser. Day eighty, fifteen days after that, is the deadline for the two appraisers to agree an umpire or ask the circuit court to appoint one. Once any two of the three sign, the amount is fixed. Now change one fact. Suppose the day thirty letter had said, explicitly, the north slope shows only pre existing wear, not hail impact, and that portion of the claim is denied. Now the north slope must be carved out of the appraisal demand and given its own path, exactly the way the plumbing claim in Maksym had to be carved out.

One honest gap before we recap. Nothing, not the statute and no case, tells you whether demanding appraisal by itself creates extra tolling of the suit clock beyond the notice to formal denial tolling the statute already gives you. In practice this rarely bites, because appraisal is only available once coverage is admitted, and an admission of coverage generally means no formal denial has happened yet. But if a carrier reverses course mid appraisal and issues a real denial, treat the interaction as an open question for counsel, not a settled rule.

Time for the recap. Subsection one m: either party demands in writing, twenty days to name appraisers, fifteen more to agree an umpire or ask the circuit court of the county of loss or property, item by item awards, any two of three bind, each side pays its own appraiser, umpire costs split fifty fifty. Kwaiser: coverage is for courts, amount of loss is for appraisers, and once coverage is admitted appraisal is mandatory. Cantina, twenty twenty four: continued processing without a formal denial equals an admission. Maksym, twenty twenty six: paying accepted items while expressly denying others is not a partial payment on the denied items. Smitham: a formal denial must be explicit and unequivocal, a partial payment does not restart the clock, and a policy cannot make tolling conditional on a denial. Subsection one q: one year after loss or the policy's longer period, tolled from notice until formal denial, a rule born in Tom Thomas in nineteen seventy six and written into the statute in nineteen ninety. Rory, two thousand five: courts enforce clear limitation periods as written, and Rory overruled Tom Thomas only on reasonableness. White, twenty eleven: contingency fee party appraisers are fine with disclosure. Dupree: awards are final except for bad faith, fraud, misconduct, or manifest mistake, and an ACV award does not automatically release the replacement cost holdback.
